questions.q: How does kind ('Kubernetes IN Docker') run a cluster's nodes?
options: Each node is a separate physical machine
Each node runs as a Docker container
Nodes run inside a single shared VM
kind does not create real nodes, only a simulation
questions.explain: kind runs each cluster node as a Docker container, which is why it starts in seconds and is easy to tear down and recreate — ideal for local development and CI.

questions.q: After running `kind create cluster`, how does `kubectl` know how to reach the new cluster without you specifying an IP address?
options: kubectl guesses the address automatically every time
kind writes connection details into your local kubeconfig file
You must manually edit /etc/hosts
kubectl only works with clusters on localhost:8080
questions.explain: Creating the cluster writes its connection details into the kubeconfig file (~/.kube/config by default), which kubectl reads to find and authenticate to the cluster.

questions.q: What is a 'context' in a kubeconfig file?
options: A Kubernetes namespace
A named entry representing one cluster plus its credentials, which kubectl can switch between
A type of Pod
The log output of a running container
questions.explain: A kubeconfig can hold several clusters at once, each as a named context. kubectl always acts against whichever context is current, and `use-context` switches between them.

questions.q: Why do contexts matter beyond local development, later in this course?
options: They don't — contexts are only relevant to local clusters
Once Northbridge has a local cluster, an AKS cluster, and an EKS cluster in the same kubeconfig, contexts prevent running a command against the wrong one
Contexts control how many replicas a Deployment runs
Contexts are a billing construct in Azure and AWS
questions.explain: With multiple clusters registered in one kubeconfig, the current context determines which cluster every kubectl command actually targets — getting this wrong means running commands against the wrong cluster.

questions.q: Which command confirms a cluster's nodes and control plane are actually healthy?
options: kubectl get nodes, checking for Ready status
kubectl config get-contexts
kind create cluster
kubectl config use-context
questions.explain: A node in Ready status confirms the control plane can reach the node, the kubelet is running, and the network between them works — a real, working cluster.
